mcqs.question: In a typical CNN image classifier, where does most of the representational power (the ability to distinguish visually complex classes) actually live?
options: In the convolutional backbone, which extracts progressively higher-level features; the classification head is usually just one or two simple layers on top
In the softmax function itself, which performs the real pattern recognition
Equally split between the backbone and the classification head by design
In the preprocessing/normalization step, since that determines input quality
mcqs.explanation: The backbone does the heavy lifting: stacked convolutional layers build up from edges to textures to object parts to whole-object concepts, producing a rich feature vector; the head merely maps that vector to class scores via one or two layers, and softmax just normalizes those scores into probabilities. Softmax (A) has no learned parameters that recognize patterns, preprocessing (D) affects input quality but doesn't perform recognition, and the split is heavily backbone-weighted, not equal (C is false).

mcqs.question: A team building a handwritten-digit classifier adds random horizontal flips as an augmentation and sees accuracy get worse. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Horizontal flips always improve image classifiers regardless of task
Horizontal flipping isn't label-preserving for digits — a flipped "6" can resemble a "9" (and vice versa), so the augmentation is injecting incorrect labels into training
The model architecture must be too small to handle augmented data
Augmentation should never be used with CNNs
mcqs.explanation: This illustrates the core caveat about augmentation: it must be genuinely label-preserving for the task, and horizontal flips are not label-preserving for digits, since flipping can transform one valid digit into what looks like a different one, corrupting the training signal. Augmentation is not universally beneficial regardless of task (A is false — that's the whole point of this example), model size isn't the cause (C), and augmentation is broadly useful with CNNs when chosen correctly (D is an overreaction).

mcqs.question: Why does an ImageNet-pretrained backbone transfer well to an unrelated task like classifying satellite crop-health images, even though ImageNet contains no satellite imagery?
options: ImageNet secretly includes satellite images alongside common objects
Transfer learning only works when the source and target domains are visually identical

The early and middle convolutional layers learn general-purpose visual features (edges, textures, shapes) that are useful across almost any visual domain, not just the specific classes ImageNet was trained on
The classification head is what transfers, not the backbone's convolutional layers
mcqs.explanation: The transferability comes from the generality of low/mid-level visual features learned by convolutional layers — edge and texture detectors are broadly useful regardless of the specific object categories in the pretraining set, which is exactly why transfer learning works even across quite different visual domains. ImageNet doesn't contain satellite imagery (A is false), transfer learning is valuable precisely because domains don't need to match exactly (C is false), and it's the backbone's convolutional layers that transfer — the classification head is typically replaced entirely (D is backwards).

mcqs.question: A medical imaging team has only 300 labeled X-rays for a new diagnosis category. Should they train a CNN from scratch or use transfer learning, and why?
options: Train from scratch, since medical images are too specialized for ImageNet-pretrained features to help at all
Train from scratch, since transfer learning requires the target domain to be photographic images
Either approach yields identical results at this data size

Transfer learning, since 300 images is far too small to train a deep CNN from random initialization without severe overfitting, and pretrained low/mid-level visual features still provide a useful starting point
mcqs.explanation: 300 labeled images is nowhere near enough to train a deep CNN's millions of parameters from scratch without severe overfitting; starting from ImageNet-pretrained weights and fine-tuning (often just the head, or with a low learning rate) is the standard, effective approach even for a specialized domain like medical imaging, because low-level visual features (edges, textures) still transfer. Claiming ImageNet features provide zero benefit for medical images (A) is an overstatement — they still help even if the domain looks different; the two approaches produce very different outcomes at this data size (C is false); transfer learning isn't restricted to photographic-only targets (D is false).

mcqs.question: A team needs to deploy an image classifier on a mobile device with strict memory and latency constraints. Which backbone characteristic should they prioritize when choosing between ResNet and EfficientNet?
options: EfficientNet's compound scaling approach, which is specifically designed to improve accuracy per unit of compute — a better fit for constrained inference budgets than a standard ResNet of comparable accuracy
ResNet, because it is always smaller than any EfficientNet variant
Backbone choice has no effect on mobile deployment feasibility
Neither backbone can run on mobile devices; only classical ML models can
mcqs.explanation: EfficientNet's whole design goal is squeezing more accuracy out of a given compute/parameter budget by jointly scaling depth, width, and resolution, which makes it a stronger fit than an equivalent-accuracy ResNet when deployment constraints (memory, latency, mobile hardware) are tight. ResNet variants aren't universally smaller (B is false — ResNet-152 is large), backbone choice materially affects deployability (C is false), and modern CNN backbones including both families run on mobile devices routinely (D is false).

mcqs.question: A team fine-tunes a pretrained ResNet on their small dataset using the same learning rate they'd use for training from scratch, and validation accuracy is worse than the original pretrained model achieved on a related benchmark. What is the most likely cause?
options: Fine-tuning a pretrained model always performs worse than training from scratch
The learning rate is too high for fine-tuning, causing large gradient updates that overwrite the pretrained features before the model can learn anything useful from the new data
The dataset must be mislabeled, since fine-tuning cannot fail for any other reason
Pretrained models cannot be fine-tuned on classification tasks, only used as fixed feature extractors
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic fine-tuning pitfall: pretrained weights already encode useful, delicately-learned features, and a from-scratch-sized learning rate causes large updates that can destroy those features in the first few steps — the standard fix is a much smaller learning rate, and often freezing early layers initially. Fine-tuning doesn't inherently underperform from-scratch training (B is false, quite the opposite in the small-data regime), there are multiple possible causes of a fine-tuning failure besides mislabeling (C is too narrow), and pretrained models are routinely fine-tuned end-to-end, not just used as frozen feature extractors (D is false).
